qualifyingPaceDelta.empty: No qualifying sessions recorded for the 2026 season yet.
qualifyingPaceDelta.methodologyBody: For every qualifying session, we take each driver's best lap — Q3 if they reached it, otherwise Q2, otherwise Q1 — and measure the % gap to that session's pole time. We average that gap across every session a driver has set a time in this season. This is descriptive, not predictive: a season-to-date average, not a forecast of future form. Source: qualifying data loaded into Supabase after every race weekend (scripts/load_race.py, via FastF1).

privacyPage.metaDescription: How PaddockIntel collects and uses your email address.
privacyPage.title: Privacy Policy
privacyPage.s1p: When you subscribe to the PaddockIntel Weekly Digest, we collect your email address and your preferred language (English, Spanish, or Portuguese) — no change there. Creating an account is separate and optional: you never need one to read the site. If you sign in with Google, we receive your name, email address, and profile picture from Google. If you sign in with email, we receive only your email address. Once signed in, we store which drivers and constructors you choose to follow — nothing else. We do not track your reading history or infer preferences you haven't explicitly set.
privacyPage.s2p: Your email address is used only to send the PaddockIntel Weekly Digest. Account data is used only to run your account: signing you in, remembering who you follow, and, in the future, ordering content on the site based on those follows. We do not sell, share, or transfer your email or account data to any third party, and we do not use it for advertising or profiling. Following someone never changes official standings, results, or rankings — only the order in which things appear for you.
privacyPage.s3p: Subscription and account records are stored in Supabase (database hosted in the United States). Emails are delivered via Resend (transactional email provider). Signing in with Google is processed by Google under its own privacy policy. All three operate under their own privacy policies and data processing agreements.
privacyPage.s4p: Every digest email contains an unsubscribe link at the bottom. Clicking it removes your address immediately and permanently. You can also contact us directly at <mail>info@paddockintel.com</mail>.
privacyPage.s5p: You can download a copy of your account data, or delete your account and all follow data immediately, from your <account>account page</account> at any time — no need to email us. If you'd rather we do it for you, contact <mail>info@paddockintel.com</mail>. Deleting your account does not affect a separate newsletter subscription made with the same email address, which is unsubscribed separately (see above).
privacyPage.s6p: paddockintel.com does not use advertising cookies or cross-site trackers. To count visits we use Cloudflare Web Analytics, which sets no cookies, stores nothing on your device and does not fingerprint visitors: it reports only aggregate data such as the page viewed, the referring site, country, browser, device type and page load speed. For this data, Cloudflare discards your IP address at its nearest data center. Our hosting provider (Cloudflare) also keeps standard, short-lived server logs (IP address, requested page) needed to operate and secure the service. The site also sets three small cookies of its own, read only by paddockintel.com and never shared: NEXT_LOCALE remembers the language of the page you're reading and expires when you close the browser; pi_box keeps, for one year, a random number from 2 to 99 and up to 12 drivers or constructors you follow without an account, so the site can order content for you (the first time you sign in, those follows can be copied to your account); and pi_subscribed records, for one year, that you subscribed to the newsletter, so subscriber articles open without asking again. Signing in sets a session cookie so the site knows you're logged in — it isn't used for tracking or advertising.
privacyPage.s7p: Questions about this policy: <mail>info@paddockintel.com</mail> or via the <about>about page</about>.

methodology.metaTitle: Delta Ribbon Methodology: How the Gap Chart Works
methodology.metaDescription: How the Delta Ribbon is built from OpenF1 timing data: what it measures, how lead changes are detected, its limits and what it does not claim.
methodology.headline: Delta Ribbon
methodology.dek: Our chart for showing how the gap between two drivers opened and closed around a lap. This page documents exactly what it computes, where the data comes from, where it falls short, and what it deliberately does not claim.

stats.racesUnit: {count, plural, one {# driver pairing} other {# driver pairings}}
stats.samplesUnit: {count, plural, one {across # race lap} other {across # race laps}}
stats.snapsUnit: {count, plural, =0 {no braids} one {# braid} other {# braids}}

s1.heading: What it shows
s1.body: Delta Ribbon is a band drawn over a circuit's outline. Its color shows which of two drivers was ahead at each point of the lap; its width shows how big the gap between them was at that point: thin means a close fight, wide means a big gap. Markers along the band flag the moments the data shows a lead change or a near-miss.

s2.heading: What is measured
s2.p1: The base number is the official gap to the race leader that OpenF1 publishes for every car, every few seconds. For each sample we take Driver B's gap minus Driver A's: the result is the gap between those two drivers. Positive means A is ahead.
s2.p2: Each sample is then placed on the lap using the position of whichever driver is ahead at that instant: we add up the distance between that car's consecutive location points and divide by the total for that lap, giving a 0–100% position independent of the track drawing. The width is square-root scaled, so a 0.3s fight still shows visible variation next to a 20s gap; the scale tops out at the race's largest gap or 8s, whichever is larger.
s2.p3: The ribbon on a circuit page draws one lap: the last lap with data, with the space between samples filled in to close the loop. The markers and the counts next to it cover the whole race, so a marker can sit on the drawn lap even though it happened on an earlier one.

s3.heading: How events are detected
s3.intro: Events are found afterwards, by scanning the same stored gap series in time order. Nothing is predicted.
s3.snapDef: The driver ahead changes between two consecutive samples.
s3.braidDef: Two or more snaps within 400 metres of each other are grouped into one hatched braid instead of separate snaps.
s3.defendDef: The trailing driver closes to under 1.0s without getting ahead, and the gap then reopens by more than 0.3s.
s3.note: A snap means the order in the timing data changed, not necessarily an overtake on track. A pit stop swings the gap by 20 seconds or more and shows up as a snap too.

s5.heading: Source and coverage
s5.intro: Everything comes from OpenF1's public endpoints (laps, car location, car data and intervals), pulled once per race by an offline script and stored in our database. Pages never call OpenF1 directly; they read the stored result. Three limits follow from that:
s5.since: 2023 onward only. OpenF1's telemetry starts with the 2023 season.
s5.onePair: One race and one pairing at a time. Each load is set up by hand. A circuit page without a load shows no ribbon.
s5.leader: No data while one of the two leads the race. The base number is a gap to the leader, and the leader has none.
s5.leaderExample: At {circuit}, the {count} laps where one of the two led ({laps}) carry {minLed}–{maxLed} samples each, against {minOther}–{maxOther} on the rest.
s5.leaderMissing: {count, plural, one {Lap {laps} has none.} other {Laps {laps} have none.}}
s5.leaderEnd: A fight for the lead itself cannot be drawn this way.

s6.heading: What it is not
s6.body: Delta Ribbon describes a session that has already finished. It does not forecast, project or model where either driver might be, and it carries no measure of uncertainty. Every color, width and marker is computed from telemetry recorded after the fact.
